title: Compare every file with every file
hook: 10 files take 45 checks. What happens when the folder holds 1,000?

doesNotKnow: that comparing every pair makes work grow with the square of the number of items

misconception: 100 times more items means about 100 times more work.
objective: The learner can explain that checking every pair of n items takes n(n-1)/2 comparisons, so doubling the items roughly quadruples the work and 1,000 files need 499,500 comparisons, about 11,100 times the work for 10 files.

claims.text: Checking every pair among n files takes n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons: 5 files → 10, 10 → 45, 20 → 190.
claims.source: Each of n files pairs with n - 1 others, and each pair is counted twice. Demo.tsx pairs(); builder ran it in Node: 10, 45, 190. The stage draws exactly that many lines.
Arithmetic (Demo.tsx pairs(1000); builder ran it in Node).

claims.text: Doubling from 10 to 20 files multiplies the pairs by 4.2, not 2; 100 times the files gives 11,100 times the work.
claims.source: 190 / 45 = 4.22; 499,500 / 45 = 11,100 (arithmetic, computed in Demo.tsx). The ratio tends to the square of the growth (10,000x for 100x) as n grows.

claims.text: Work that grows with the square of the input hits a wall long before the input looks big.
claims.source: Follows from c1-c3: n(n-1)/2 is Theta(n^2) (CLRS 3.1 asymptotic notation). Stated qualitatively.

recall.question: A program that compares every pair of photos takes 1 second for 1,000 photos. About how long for 10,000 photos?
recall.why: Pairs grow with the square: 10 times the photos means about 100 times the pairs, so about 100 seconds.
